sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and the Initial Problem Representation
sections.description: Introduces the patient’s presenting symptoms, physical findings, and the key multisystem clues that framed the case as more than isolated nutritional anaemia. This section should teach learners how to construct a problem representation and recognize red flags for an inherited multisystem disorder in a young adult.
subtopics: Progressive fatigue, weakness, exertional dyspnoea, weight loss, and decline in functional status over 5 years
Acute worsening over 3 months and its implications for urgency and severity assessment
Physical examination findings: pallor, icterus, premature greying, knuckle hyperpigmentation, bald tongue, thoracic scoliosis, thenar atrophy, hepatomegaly, and reduced basal breath sounds
Why premature ageing features in a woman in her late 20s are diagnostically important
Identifying a multisystem syndrome: haematologic, hepatic, pulmonary, neurologic, and skeletal involvement
Constructing the initial problem representation: young adult with pancytopenia, ineffective erythropoiesis, organ fibrosis, and premature ageing stigmata
Clinical red flags that should prompt consideration of telomere biology disorders even without the classic mucocutaneous triad

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Workup: Interpreting the Haematologic, Hepatic, Pulmonary, and Neurometabolic Findings
sections.description: Details the investigations performed and explains how each result contributed to understanding the disease process. The focus is on interpreting the workup in a stepwise, clinically meaningful way rather than listing data.
subtopics: CBC and reticulocyte count: pancytopenia with low reticulocyte response as a clue to ineffective erythropoiesis or marrow failure
Peripheral smear interpretation: dimorphic red cells, basophilic stippling, Cabot rings, and hypersegmented neutrophils
Biochemical evidence of severe vitamin B12 and folate deficiency and the concept of megaloblastic ineffective erythropoiesis
Iron profile with elevated iron and ferritin in ineffective erythropoiesis
Bone marrow findings: trilineage haematopoiesis, erythroid hyperplasia, increased iron stores, and absence of malignancy or overt dysplasia
Haemolysis markers, DAT positivity, and why these did not fully support immune haemolytic anaemia
Evaluation for malabsorption and pernicious-type physiology: endoscopy and reduced parietal cells on duodenal/gastric histology
Assessment of hepatosplenomegaly and liver disease: ultrasound and transient elastography demonstrating steatosis and cirrhosis/hepatic fibrosis
Pulmonary assessment through PET-CT showing ground-glass opacities, fibrotic change, and subpleural atelectatic abnormalities consistent with pulmonary fibrosis
Inflammatory, autoimmune, and infectious testing: what was excluded and why this mattered
Associated systemic findings: osteoporosis, vitamin D deficiency, secondary hyperparathyroidism, electrolyte derangements, recurrent fractures
Electrodiagnostic evidence of asymmetric sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy and its relevance to the overall syndrome

sections.section_title: From Differential Diagnosis to Unifying Syndrome: Why a Telomere Biology Disorder Was Suspected
sections.description: Walks through the clinical reasoning that moved the team from common acquired causes toward a rare inherited disorder. This section should emphasize diagnostic synthesis, competing explanations, and the logic of ruling in a telomere biology disorder.
subtopics: Initial differential diagnosis for pancytopenia, fatigue, weight loss, and hepatosplenomegaly in a young adult
Nutritional deficiency as an early leading explanation: what it explained well and what it did not
Autoimmune cytopenia and connective tissue disease: significance and limits of a positive DAT with negative broader serologies
Bone marrow failure syndromes versus infiltrative, malignant, and infectious causes
Approach to unexplained hepatic fibrosis and pulmonary fibrosis in a young patient
Recognizing disproportionate disease burden after correction of reversible deficiencies
The diagnostic importance of combining premature greying, cytopenia, osteoporosis, liver fibrosis, and pulmonary fibrosis
How telomere biology disorders can present without classic dyskeratosis congenita mucocutaneous features
Variable penetrance, adult-onset presentation, absence of family history, and the possibility of de novo or incompletely penetrant inherited disease
Formulating a unifying diagnosis rather than accepting multiple disconnected organ-specific diagnoses

sections.section_title: PARN and Telomere Biology Disorders: Essential Pathophysiology and Genetic Interpretation
sections.description: Provides the focused background biology necessary to understand the case, including telomere maintenance, the clinical spectrum of telomere biology disorders, and how a monoallelic PARN variant can plausibly explain this phenotype. It should also teach learners how to interpret a Variant of Uncertain Significance in clinical context.
subtopics: Telomere structure, telomere shortening, cellular senescence, and stem-cell vulnerability
Telomerase complex components and the biology of telomere maintenance
Definition and spectrum of telomere biology disorders, with dyskeratosis congenita as the prototype
Classic dyskeratosis congenita triad versus atypical adult presentations dominated by marrow, liver, or lung disease
Why highly proliferative tissues such as bone marrow, mucosa, hair follicles, and hepatocytes are affected
PARN function as a deadenylase and its role in TERC 3-prime-end maturation and telomerase biology
Phenotypic distinctions between biallelic PARN-related disease and monoallelic PARN-associated pulmonary fibrosis and/or bone marrow failure
Interpretation of the identified variant c.613T>C (p.Cys205Arg): conserved residue, R3H domain location, rarity, and in silico deleterious predictions
Applying ACMG/AMP concepts to a VUS: PM1, PM2, PP2, and PP3 supportive evidence
How genotype-phenotype correlation can support a clinical diagnosis even when a variant remains formally uncertain
The possible interaction between severe vitamin B12 deficiency and a genetically vulnerable marrow
Role of telomere length testing and next-generation sequencing in confirming suspected telomere biology disorders

sections.section_title: Management, Follow-up, and Clinical Lessons for Practice
sections.description: Explains the treatment decisions made in this case, the rationale for supportive care, and the broader implications for surveillance, counselling, and long-term management of telomere biology disorders. The section should conclude with the key take-home messages for trainees.
subtopics: Immediate treatment of severe vitamin B12 deficiency: intravenous cyanocobalamin regimen and expected haematologic response
Supportive management of symptomatic anaemia with transfusion
Adjunctive correction of folate deficiency, vitamin D deficiency, calcium deficiency, and electrolyte abnormalities
Management of osteoporosis, bone pain, fractures, and rehabilitation with physiotherapy
Why treatment remained supportive despite identification of a likely telomere biology disorder
Monitoring for progression of cytopenias and evolution toward bone marrow failure
Surveillance of hepatic and pulmonary fibrosis in suspected or confirmed telomere biology disorders
Genetic counselling for the patient and family, including uncertainty around a monoallelic VUS and implications for relatives
Potential advanced therapies in telomere biology disorders: haematopoietic stem cell transplantation and organ transplantation considerations
Emerging but not yet definitive therapies such as androgen-based telomere-directed treatment
Short-term outcome in this patient: symptomatic improvement and stable counts at 2-week follow-up
Clinical pearls: when to suspect a telomere biology disorder, why classical features may be absent, and why early recognition changes surveillance and management
